iSummicron

Real-lens bokeh for phone portraits

Photographers call the look of the out-of-focus parts of a picture bokeh. A phone's portrait mode makes it by blurring the background with plain round discs. A real lens doesn't. Its blur spots have bright rims, and toward the frame edge they turn into eggs and cat's eyes that swirl around the centre.

iSummicron ray-traces real lens designs to get those shapes, then paints them into your photo using its depth map. This page shows where the shapes come from and how they get into the picture.

How blur forms, step by step

A lens bends every ray that leaves a point of light so they all meet again at one spot. The camera's sensor sits at a fixed distance behind the lens. If the rays meet exactly on the sensor, you get a sharp dot. If they meet before it, they have spread out again by the time they arrive, and the dot becomes a disc.

The pattern that one point of light leaves on the sensor has a name: the point spread function, or PSF. This page mostly calls it the blur shape. Real lenses also have aberrations: small imperfections in how they bend the rays.

The four steps below walk through this with the real lens designs. The ray paths inside the lens and every blur spot on the right come from the traced data.

The bar under the drawing follows the light. First it moves the light from the 0.7 m focus distance out to 20 m, straight ahead. Then it moves the light from the centre of the frame to the corner, and then around the frame. The bar is spaced by blur, not by metres, so most of its first part is spent below a few metres, where the blur changes most. It moves only while the picture changes and stops when the picture pauses. Drag it, or use the arrow keys, to explore by hand.

reaches the sensor blocked by a front rim blocked by the stop or a rear rim where it stops
On the sensor
The light's journey: ● holding

How to read the drawing: the light's side is not to scale. Real distances run from 0.7 m to 20 m, while the lens is a few centimetres long. The lens, the ray paths through it and the gap to the sensor are drawn to scale from the trace. The inset magnifies the last few millimetres before the sensor.

Shapes across the frame

These are the blur shapes the renderer uses: the 35 mm lens by default, the 50 mm with --lens 50. There is one per ring of the frame, counted from the centre out to the corner, and per distance. Each is drawn with the outward direction pointing up.

Near the centre they are round discs. Toward the corner, the lens rims clip the cone of light from below and above, and aberrations bunch the surviving rays into bright edges.

The traced 35 mm lens also has a faint horizontal streak at close range. It is a fan of rays from the edge of the aperture, the opening that lets light through the lens. It is real lens behaviour, so it stays in.

Brightness uses a square-root scale so that faint parts show.

How the shapes are traced

The blur shapes are made once, offline, with optiland, an open-source Python ray tracer. A ray tracer is a program that follows rays of light through a lens, one surface at a time. Nothing is traced while you render a photo: the renderer loads a finished set of shapes, the 35 mm by default or the 50 mm with --lens 50. A custom set built with the same scripts loads with --tensor. The build scripts ship with the project, so anyone can re-trace them.

  1. Start from a public lens design

    35 mm f/2: an 8-element design ray-traced from the expired US patent 3,006,249, Example II, using optiland. 50 mm f/2: the classic six-element double-Gauss that ships as an optiland sample (MIT licence). Each is scaled to its focal length at f/2 and traced in green light (550 nm). Neither is a copy of a current commercial lens.

  2. Give every glass surface a rim

    Patents list curvatures and spacings, but not how big each piece of glass is. So the clear opening of every surface is set by a simple stated rule, then trimmed so that each element is thick enough at its edge to be made. These rims are what clip the light toward the frame edge. Keep in mind that they are an assumption, not a measurement.

  3. Focus at 0.7 m and freeze the sensor

    The sensor distance is solved so that a point at 0.7 m is sharpest on axis (at the centre of the frame). Then it stays fixed for every other distance, just like a real camera that has focused.

  4. Trace a dense grid of rays per spot

    This is done for 12 positions from the centre to the corner and 10 distances from 0.98 m to 20 m. For each one, a dense, even grid of rays is traced from the point light (about 0.8–0.9 million reach the sensor per on-axis spot, fewer toward the corner). Rays that hit any rim are dropped. The pattern of where the survivors land on the sensor is the blur shape.

  5. Turn ray hits into a pixel kernel

    A kernel is a small grid of pixels that holds one blur shape. Hits are counted into a 183 × 183 pixel kernel at the pixel size of a photo 5712 pixels on its long edge, with the outward direction pointing up. Nothing is cropped, clipped or smoothed: the box is sized to hold the whole shape, including long flare tails.

  6. Check the result

    The disc size on axis is checked against an independent scan of single rays across the whole aperture (within 3%). At least 99.5% of the light must land inside the box. And a fixed random seed makes the trace repeat exactly. Both lenses pass.

The focus slot (0.7 m) is stored as a single bright pixel rather than a traced spot. The photo already holds the in-focus detail, so the renderer's job there is to leave it alone.

The render pipeline, step by step

A depth map records how far away each part of the scene is. The renderer takes a portrait photo and its depth map, decides how far out of focus each pixel is, and mixes the blurs the lens gives at the nearest traced distances. These are the steps, in order.

  1. Depth from the photo

    Portrait photos carry a depth map from the phone's depth sensor. iSummicron reads it and scales it to the full image. It then lightly smooths the depth sensor's stair-steps, guided by the photo's own edges. If a photo has no depth map, a machine-learning depth estimator fills in.

  2. Tap to focus

    You pick the focus point. Its depth (a 3 × 3 median, to ignore single noisy pixels) becomes the in-focus distance. With no tap, the depth of the nearest 2% of the frame is used.

  3. Depth becomes blur amount

    Blur depends on diopters, not metres. A diopter is 1 / distance. That is why the background a few metres behind a subject is already nearly as blurry as the far horizon.

    For each pixel, iSummicron takes the diopter distance from the focus point and maps it onto the lens's 11 distance slots. A pixel 1 diopter behind your subject is placed where a light 1 diopter behind the lens's own 0.7 m focus would sit.

    By default (--depth-gain auto) this mapping is one-to-one (a gain of 1), so the blur is physical rather than tuned per photo. --depth-gain scales it up or down. Content in front of the focus point and behind it gets the same blur for the same diopter distance. This applies with the depth sensor's map. With estimated depth, a simpler straight mapping in metres is used.

  4. Blur in depth layers

    Each of the 11 distances is one layer, and each layer blurs the whole photo. A pixel then takes a smooth mix of at most three neighbouring layers, with weights that always add up to one, so there are no hard steps between near and far. Layers that no pixel needs are skipped. How the blur is put back together shows this step by step.

  5. The subject stays sharp

    Pixels at the focus depth take the first layer, whose "blur" is a single pixel, so it returns the photo unchanged. At the very end, pixels close to focus are faded back to the original photo (the snap, below).

  6. Blend across the frame

    The frame is split into 12 rings from the centre to the corner. Each pixel blends the shapes of the two nearest rings, weighted by its distance between them. Going around the circle, there is no blending (see the next step).

  7. Turn the shape to face outward

    The lens shapes are stored once per ring, with outward pointing up. The renderer turns them to face away from the centre, but in 8 fixed steps of 45°. Every pixel in a 45° slice of the frame gets the same turn.

    A shape can therefore be up to 22.5° off its true angle, and its orientation changes by 45° from one slice to the next.

    Tests with 16 and 32 steps reduced the angle error but made a render about 1.5× and 2.4× slower (35 mm lens, 2048 px; see Under the hood). In side-by-side renders viewed normally (tone-mapped), 8, 16 and 32 steps looked the same, so the setting stays at 8.

    The frame is cut into 8 slices of 45° around its centre. Each slice uses the shape turned to the slice's middle angle (arrows). To see the snapping, try the "Renderer (8 steps)" switch in step 4 of the animation above.

  8. Highlights get their own pass

    Bright points such as bulbs, reflections and sun glints are split off before blurring. A local "is this a small bright spot?" test favours isolated lights over broad bright areas.

    These highlights are blurred with the same lens shapes and the same layer weights, carrying a fixed 2× the light's own energy (every lens shape is L1-normalised: its pixels add up to one). A bulb therefore stays a bright, well-defined shape, and big and small shapes carry the same light. The two parts are added back together in linear light (pixel values proportional to the real amount of light, before any tone curve), before the final tone step, which keeps the photo's own look. The next section shows both parts step by step.

Kernel sizes are stored for a photo 5712 pixels on its long edge and scaled with the output size, so a smaller render gets proportionally smaller shapes.

How the blur is put back together

Blur shapes and convolution are the familiar part. The new part is how the blurred pieces become one picture again. Below is the kitchen photo before and after. Every background pixel got a different blur shape, yet there are no seams and no dark gaps, and the subject is left alone. Drag across the picture to compare.

The photoThe render
PhotoRender

Default 35 mm lens, focus tapped on the subject, rendered at 2048 px on the long edge and shown smaller here.

In one sentence: the photo is read along two hidden axes, how far and how bright. It is blurred once per distance layer and put back together with weights that always add up to one. The highlights ride the same weights in a second buffer and are added in before the picture is brought back down to screen brightness.

One photo, two hidden axes

A Portrait photo carries two extra maps. One says how far away each pixel is (from the depth sensor). The other, the HDR gain map, says how much brighter than white each pixel really was. The renderer slices the photo along both.

Here 20% of the pixels are brighter than white in at least one colour channel. The brightest reach 3.45× white. The depth sensor's map ends at 2.46 m.

Part 1: how far

Distance becomes a slot position. Blur follows diopters (1 / distance), not metres. Each pixel's diopter gap from the tapped subject is placed on the lens's 11 traced distances, the slots. Content in front of the subject is placed like content the same number of diopters behind it. In this room nothing gets past slot 6: the farthest pixel sits between slots 5 and 6. So 4 of the 11 layers are never needed.

Every layer gets the lens shape. Each of the 7 layers that run blurs the whole photo with the shapes the lens gives at that distance. The shape also changes across the frame: two rings are blended, and one of 8 wedges sets the direction. Layer 0 is the focus slot. Its "shape" is a single pixel, so it returns the photo unchanged. The photo is not cut into layers first. The cut comes afterwards, from each layer's weight map.

Animation A: distance layers, from depth to one picture
Layer:

The pictures in both animations are rebuilt in your browser from quarter-size copies of the renderer's own layers, weights and tone curve. The rebuilt sum matches the renderer's sum to within 1.5 of 255 on average (99% of pixels within 8), and the rebuilt final picture matches the renderer's output to within 1.6 on average.

The blend, up close

Which layers a pixel takes. A pixel between two slots takes the layer on each side plus the one just nearer: three in all (two next to the focus slot). The middle one always gets one half. The other half slides smoothly from the nearer layer to the farther one as the pixel's distance moves across the gap. So the mix leans toward the nearer layers: a pixel sitting exactly on a slot gets half that slot's layer and half the nearer one. Here 55% of the pixels mix three layers and 35% mix two.

Why the weights add up to one. After the raw weights are found, each pixel's weights are divided by their own total. Whatever the distance, the shares add up to exactly one, so the pixel is fully accounted for, once.

Pick a pixel

Drag the marker, or click or tap anywhere, for the weights (arrow keys work too), or step through the 8 numbered points. Their values were taken at full size; values for other spots come from a smaller depth map and are approximate at this preview size, especially along the subject's outline. The depth slider moves the pixel to a new depth so you can watch the three bars trade places. The blur shapes are the renderer's own, shown as they are, tails included, on a square-root scale.

Results are mixed, shapes are not. Each blurred layer is multiplied by its weight map and added to a running picture. A coverage meter fills up alongside and ends at exactly one at every pixel. No in-between shape is ever invented: the finished blurs are mixed. At a lamp, layers 4, 5 and 6 add up to one wider rim, not a disc of middle size. Every shape adds up to one and every pixel's weights add up to one, so the mix never brightens or darkens a pixel. A flat wall stays the same flat wall.

The subject snaps back. Last, pixels near the focus distance are faded back to the original photo. The fade is full at the focus distance and gone by the next slot. In between, a pixel is the sharp photo and a light blur added together. The cut at the subject's outline is only as good as the depth map: stray hairs that the sensor placed on the background are blurred with it.

Part 2: how bright

Brightness becomes a split. On a normal screen the lamps are just white. Pull the exposure down and they turn out to be up to 3.45 times brighter than white. The renderer lifts out the small, very bright spots (0.159% of the pixels here) and keeps them in a buffer of their own. The whole pixel value moves, not only the part above the threshold. Everything else stays in the main buffer, with dark holes where the lamps were. This is one buffer split in two, not one copy per brightness level.

Animation B: highlights, from the gain map to the screen

The crop is 500 × 160 pixels at full render size, just above the middle of the frame. In steps 1 to 4 the picture is shown at plain exposure: values above white are cut off at white, so use the exposure slider to see them. Step 5 shows the real tone step. Its comparison puts both sides through that same display; the no-gain-map render also used a lower highlight threshold (1.0) and its own final picture uses a different tone step, so only the blur in real light is compared.

The highlights ride the same weights. The highlight buffer goes through the same loop with the same layer weights, into a second running picture. At the end the two are added. The blurred lamps land in the dark holes that the split left behind. The highlight shapes carry twice the lamp's own light: a fixed look choice that keeps blurred lamps bright. So the highlights are blurred from their real HDR brightness, with a gain of 2. In this crop that adds 14.1% light; over the whole frame, 0.5%.

Back down to the screen. Only now, with the blur finished in real light, is the picture brought back to screen brightness. The curve is measured from the photo itself, its HDR version against its normal version, so the render keeps the photo's own tone. A lamp that is blurred first and compressed second stays a bright disc. Compress it first and it becomes a grey one. In-focus pixels come out close to the original but not identical: the tone step differs from the phone's own normal version by about 3 of 255 on average.

What this does not do, and what it costs

  • No occlusion. A blurred background can pick up a little subject colour in a thin band along the outline.
  • Hard wedges. Shapes turn in 8 steps of 45°, so a shape can be up to 22.5° off its true direction.
  • A mix of finished blurs. A pixel between slots gets a mix of nearby layers' blurs, leaning toward the nearer ones, not a blur of in-between size.
  • Depth sets the ceiling. The depth sensor's map stops at 2.46 m in this photo, so nothing here reaches the larger blurs of the far slots.
  • Cost. The layer blurs are most of the run time: 81–91% of a render at 2048 px, depending on lens and HDR.

Under the hood

The same pipeline in more detail, with the formulas the renderer uses. Each part opens on its own. Distances are in metres (m), and diopters (D) are 1 / distance.

Depth to diopters to a lens distanceHow a depth-map value becomes one of the lens's traced distances.

The focus anchor. The anchor is the depth at your tap: the median of a 3 × 3 patch, so a single noisy pixel can't move it. With no tap, the anchor is the depth of the nearest 2% of the frame (the 2nd percentile).

The mapping. For every pixel at depth z:

dp = | 1/z − 1/anchor | diopters away from focus e = min(gain × dp, 1/0.7 − 1/20) capped at 1.3786 D z_t = 1 / (1/0.7 − e) equivalent distance, 0.7 … 20 m

z_t is where a light would have to sit, in front of the traced lens focused at 0.7 m, to be just as far out of focus as this pixel is from your anchor. Everything at the anchor's depth lands exactly on 0.7 m, the in-focus slot. That includes every pixel at that depth, not only the one you tapped. Depth values that are missing or invalid are also treated as in focus.

The gain is auto by default, which means 1. That makes the mapping physical: one diopter in your scene is one diopter for the lens. --depth-gain N multiplies it.

A worked example with gain 1: you focus on a subject at 1 m. A wall at 3 m is 1 − 0.333 = 0.667 D away, so it is placed at 1 / (1.4286 − 0.667) ≈ 1.31 m on the lens's distance scale. A very distant background is 1.0 D away and is placed at about 2.33 m. Anything more than 1.3786 D from focus gets the 20 m blur, the largest the lens makes.

Front and back fold together. Because of the absolute value, a pixel 0.5 D in front of the anchor gets exactly the same blur as one 0.5 D behind it. There are no traced slots in front of the 0.7 m focus yet (see Objects in front of the focus).

Estimated depth. When a photo has no depth-sensor map, the machine-learning estimate is relative rather than in metres, so a simpler straight mapping in metres is used instead.

Depth layers and their weights11 layers, at most three per pixel, weights that always add up to one.

11 layers, one per traced distance: 0.70, 0.98, 1.37, 1.91, 2.68, 3.74, 5.23, 7.32, 10.23, 14.30 and 20.0 m. Each is about 1.4× the one before. Layer 0, at 0.7 m, is the in-focus layer.

The weight curves. Layer d's weight rises from slot d−1 to slot d, stays at 1 from slot d to slot d+1, and falls back to 0 by slot d+2. The rises and falls are smooth S-curves (3t² − 2t³) in metres. Then each pixel's weights are divided by their sum, so they always add up to exactly one. Below 0.7 m, layer 0 takes everything; beyond 20 m, layer 10 does.

Weights of the 11 layers against z_t, drawn on a diopter scale. The in-focus layer is teal.

What a pixel sees. Between slots k and k+1 (for k ≥ 1), three layers overlap: layers k−1, k and k+1, with weights 0.5(1−s), 0.5 and 0.5s, where s is the S-curve of the pixel's position between the two slots. So the mix leans toward the nearer layers: a pixel exactly on slot k is half layer k−1 and half layer k. Between slot 0 and slot 1 only two overlap: 1/(1+s) on the in-focus layer and s/(1+s) on layer 1.

Shapes are not mixed; results are. Each layer blurs the frame with its own slot's traced shapes. The blurred results are then multiplied by the layer weights and added. No in-between shape is ever made up.

Skipping. A layer that no pixel gives a weight of at least 0.01 is skipped entirely. If skipping leaves a pixel with less than 2% total weight, it takes the result of the nearest layer that ran.

Rings across the frame: the radial blend12 rings from centre to corner, a linear blend between the nearest two.

Radial position is a pixel's distance from the image centre divided by the half-diagonal, so 0 is the centre and 1.0 is a corner.

12 rings. Their edges sit at 0, 0.151, 0.302, 0.426, 0.522, 0.603, 0.674, 0.739, 0.798, 0.853, 0.905, 0.953 and 1.0. The outer ten rings have equal areas, and the central disc is split in two. Each ring's shapes are traced at the midpoint of the ring, from 0.075 to 0.977.

The blend. A pixel takes the shapes of the two ring midpoints on either side of it, with straight-line weights by distance between them. Inside the first midpoint, or beyond the last, it uses that one ring alone. A ring is skipped when its weight is below 0.01 everywhere in the wedge.

Keeping the light. Each layer's blurred result is divided by its total ring weight, so the ring blend never brightens or darkens a pixel.

8 hard angular wedges and the rotationHow one stored shape per ring is turned to face away from the centre.

One orientation is stored. The traced shapes have no angle axis. Each is stored once per ring and distance, with the outward direction pointing up.

Wedges. Each pixel's angle around the image centre puts it in one of 8 wedges of 45°. In image coordinates (y pointing down):

a = floor( (atan2(y − cy, x − cx) + π) / 2π × 8 ) mod 8 θ_a = (a + 0.5) × 45° − 180° wedge centre: −157.5°, −112.5° … +157.5° rot = −(θ_a + 90°) turns "up" to point at the wedge centre

The rotation turns the shape about its centre with bilinear sampling, clips any negative values to zero, and re-normalises it. Every pixel in a wedge uses the same turned shape. Wedges are not blended, so a pixel's shape is off its true angle by up to ±22.5°, and the error follows a sawtooth around the frame.

Per pixel, that is at most 3 layers × 2 rings × 1 wedge = 6 shapes. The highlight pass uses the same turned shape. The single-pixel in-focus shape is never turned.

Why 8. More wedges cost time: about 1.5× at 16 and 2.4× at 32 (measured, table below).

WedgesWorst angle errorRender time (35 mm lens, 2048 px)
8 (used)±22.5°22.5 s
16±11.25°34.7 s
32±5.6°53.5 s

In side-by-side tone-mapped renders, the three settings looked the same by eye, so the renderer stays at 8.

How the focus point stays sharpThree locks in a row, all pointing at the untouched photo.
  1. Diopter lock. A pixel at the anchor's depth has dp = 0, so it maps to z_t = 0.7 m, the in-focus slot.
  2. Layer lock. At that slot, the in-focus layer has weight 1 and every other layer 0. Its shape is a single pixel in all 12 rings, and blurring with a single pixel returns the photo unchanged. It is applied without rotation, and it stays an exact single pixel when the output is made smaller.
  3. In-focus snap. At the very end, pixels near focus are faded back to the original photo:
    α = cos²( π/2 × min(r / 0.10, 1) ) out = α × photo + (1 − α) × blurred
    Here r is the pixel's place on the slot axis, running from 0 at slot 0 to 1 at slot 10 in equal steps per slot. So the snap is full at the anchor and gone by slot 1.

How wide the sharp zone is. The snap reaches zero at slot 1, 0.4069 D from focus. There the pixel is half sharp, half layer-1 blur. The in-focus layer's share reaches zero at slot 2, 0.6979 D from focus. Past that, only blur remains.

With the default gain of 1 those are real diopters. For a subject at 1 m, the snap ends at about 0.71 m in front and 1.69 m behind. The sharp share ends at about 0.59 m in front and 3.3 m behind. A larger --depth-gain narrows the zone.

The weak point is the anchor itself. A tap on a depth edge, or on glass that the depth sensor reads instead of what is behind it, puts the sharp zone on the wrong surface.

Bright-stamp highlightsHow small bright lights are split off and painted as lens shapes.

The split. On the linear image, each pixel gets a bright weight:

bw = smoothstep from T − 0.2 to T + 0.2 of brightness × (0.10 + 0.90 × clip(tophat / p99(tophat), 0, 1)) tophat = brightness − grey_opening(brightness, 31 px) bright = image × bw diffuse = image − bright

The top-hat keeps bright features smaller than about 31 px and drops broad bright areas such as a window or a white wall. The 0.10 floor means broad bright areas still count a little. T is 1.0, SDR white. When the tone step reproduces the photo's own tone curve, T is raised to 1.1 × the HDR brightness that the curve maps to 90% white, if that is higher than 1.0.

The stamp. Kernels are always L1-normalised: each lens shape's pixels add up to one, so a blur with one shape keeps the total light. The bright part is blurred with the same turned lens shape as the rest, times 2. Its total light is kept and doubled, so a bulb reads as a bright, well-defined shape. --bright-stamp-gain changes the 2×.

Putting it back. Both parts go through the same layer and ring weights. They are added together in linear light, before the final checks, the in-focus snap and the tone step. Pixels on the in-focus layer skip the split, so in-focus highlights pass through untouched.

Key numbersThe constants in one place.
ItemValue

Why HDR matters for bokeh

Out-of-focus lights only look like lights if the renderer knows how bright they really are. A normal (SDR) photo stores everything brighter than white as plain white, 1.0. Spread a clipped bulb over a big blur shape and its light is shared across many pixels, so it comes out as a dim, soft disc.

An iPhone Portrait photo also carries an HDR gain map, which records how much brighter the highlights really were. In the kitchen photo below, the brightest input highlights reach about 3.5× white instead of stopping at 1.0, and about 12% of the frame is brighter than white (20% in at least one colour channel). With that light restored, the blurred lamps stay bright and keep their shape.

Both crops: the plain default render (default 35 mm lens, no lens flags) at 2048 px on the long edge. The left one adds only --hdr-source none.

Where it sits in the pipeline: load the photo (with its gain map) → blur in linear light → tone step back to a normal SDR picture that keeps the photo's own look. The blur happens on the restored, brighter-than-white values; only the final picture is brought back to SDR.

The --hdr-source setting:

  • auto (the default): uses the gain map when the photo has one and the macOS HDR loader is available, otherwise falls back to none and says so in one line.
  • macos: always use the macOS HDR loader, with no fallback. It needs macOS and the optional hdr-macos install extra.
  • none: plain SDR. It works on any platform.

The gain-map path needs macOS today, because it reads the photo with Apple's own image framework. On other platforms renders are SDR. They still work; the brightest lights are just dimmer. The difference is modest and shows mostly on the brightest lights. The output file is a normal SDR image, so you don't need an HDR display to see it.

Subject edges and occlusion

In a real photo, the subject blocks some of the background's blur: a light just behind someone's shoulder is partly hidden by it. The default render does not model this. Background blur is free to cross the subject's outline.

With real-lens blur shapes this changes only a hairline along the subject's outline, which is not visible at normal viewing. A stricter option, --occlusion-compositing on, stacks the depth layers front to back so that nearer layers cover farther ones. It costs about 30–60% more render time (1.3–1.6×), so it is off by default. It is still there for scenes with a very bright light directly behind an outline, the one case where it should help most.

Guided depth and the in-focus snap already keep the subject's edge clean. These are the terms used here and above:

Guided depth
The depth map is smoothed with the photo's own edges as a guide, so depth steps line up with the real outline.
In-focus snap
At the very end, pixels at or near the focus depth are faded back to the original photo, so the subject stays as shot.
Linear light
Pixel values proportional to the real amount of light, before any tone curve. Blurring and adding up light is only correct in these units.

Objects in front of the focus

Today, iSummicron only knows how far a pixel is from focus in diopters, not which side it is on. A light that is a given number of diopters in front of your subject is blurred exactly like one the same number of diopters behind it, and with the same lens shapes: the ones traced behind the focus. Both sides stop growing at the same maximum blur, 1.38 diopters from focus. With the default settings, for a subject at 0.7 m that means anything nearer than about 0.36 m gets the maximum blur; for a subject at 1 m, anything nearer than about 0.42 m.

A real lens is different in front of focus:

  • The shapes flip. In front of focus the image of the lens opening is turned over, so tails and cat-eye cuts point inward instead of outward.
  • The rim character swaps. The leftover aberrations that give a disc a bright rim on one side of focus give it a soft edge on the other. So a lens with bright-rimmed “soap-bubble” discs on one side of focus has softer discs on the other.
  • A blurry foreground drapes over the subject. A real out-of-focus object near the camera spreads softly across the sharp subject behind it, like a veil. The renderer does not do this yet.

Planned for 0.5.2: trace real in-front-of-focus shapes with optiland, and have the renderer pick the front or the back shapes depending on which side of focus each pixel is.

Christmas-lights demo

This is a synthetic test scene. It has about 585 point lights in rings, strands and a tree, most at 20 m and some at 1.9 m. They sit behind a gold bauble in focus at 0.7 m. The scene has a fixed depth map and no photo, so only the blur differs.

Every version runs through the same blur engine. The "plain disc" versions use round discs sized to match each real lens, which is roughly what phone portrait modes do. They were made for this comparison only and are not a renderer option.

The demo's lights use the renderer's default highlight setting: each bulb is spread with the L1-normalised shape, so it keeps its own total light, times a fixed 2×. Big and small blur shapes therefore carry the same light.

The input comes first. The round and oval lights below are made by the blur. In the input every light is a single sharp point, too small to see at page size, so the input panels draw them larger.

Bottom-left corner, 2× zoom

The full frame

35 mm f/2 (default)

What to look at: the corners. The wider lens clips much harder at the edge (under a fifth of the light gets through at the corner). Its corner shapes shrink into small rounded boxes with bright sides.

50 mm f/2

What to look at: the spinning bokeh. Toward the edges the shapes flatten along the line to the centre, so the rings of lights seem to swirl.

Top-left corner, close-up

Honest limits

  • Turning in 8 steps. Shapes face outward to within ±22.5°, and the orientation changes by 45° from one slice to the next. In normal (tone-mapped) viewing, 8, 16 and 32 steps looked the same; more steps cost render time.
  • Blur crosses the subject's outline. By default, background blur is not stopped at the subject's outline. With real-lens blur this changes only a hairline, not visible at normal viewing; see Subject edges. The stricter --occlusion-compositing on costs about 30–60% more render time (1.3–1.6×).
  • HDR needs macOS. The gain-map path that restores real highlight brightness runs on macOS only. Elsewhere renders are SDR and the brightest lights come out dimmer.
  • No edge darkening yet. The trace records how much light gets through at each position (down to roughly 18–28% in the corners), and the clipping changes the shape. The renderer does not yet use this to darken the corners: each shape keeps its full brightness.
  • Front and back look the same. Blur in front of the focus point uses the same shapes as blur behind it, so lenses whose foreground and background bokeh differ can't be shown yet. See Objects in front of the focus; real front shapes are planned for 0.5.2.
  • One colour of light. The trace uses green light only, so there is no colour fringing in the bokeh.
  • Assumed rims. The glass rim sizes follow a stated rule rather than a measured lens, and the lens designs are public classics, not a specific current product.
  • Depth is the weak link. The phone's depth sensor can read a window instead of what is behind it, and the blur can only be as right as the depth. In the kitchen photo its map stops at 2.46 m.
  • A mix of finished blurs. A pixel between two traced distances gets a weighted mix of nearby layers' blurs, leaning toward the nearer ones, not a blur of in-between size.
  • The layer blurs cost the most. They take 81–91% of a render at 2048 px.
Lens designs: the expired US patent 3,006,249, Example II (public domain), and the optiland DoubleGauss sample (MIT). Ray tracing: optiland. The Christmas-lights scene and the charts are synthetic. The two HDR crops and the pictures in How the blur is put back together come from the project's sample kitchen photo or maps derived from it, re-encoded from pixels with all metadata removed.
